title: How do you implement read/write splitting at the application level (route writes to the primary and reads to a replica) — e.g. an `AbstractRoutingDataSource` that selects the datasource from a key set per request or driven by `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` — and what must you watch for (replication lag causing stale reads, so reads that must be fresh are routed back to the primary)?
shortTitle: Read/write splitting at the application level with AbstractRoutingDataSource

s1_definition.profdef: Application-level read/write splitting routes write operations to the primary and read operations to a replica using a single logical datasource that dynamically chooses the physical connection. In Spring this is typically a custom `AbstractRoutingDataSource` whose routing key is derived per request or from `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, with a `ThreadLocal` holding the current route. The main hazard is replication lag causing stale reads, so any read that must reflect a just-committed write is explicitly routed back to the primary.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank has one main ledger (primary) for all changes and several photocopy desks (replicas) for quick enquiries. A smart receptionist (the routing datasource) looks at each request: "Are you changing money? Go to the main ledger. Just checking a balance? Go to a photocopy desk." But if you just made a change, the receptionist knows the photocopies may be a second behind, so for your immediate enquiry she sends you back to the main ledger so you always see your own change.
s1_definition.oneliner: Mark reads as readOnly so a routing datasource sends them to a replica and everything else to the primary, but send must-be-fresh reads back to the primary because of lag.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Application-level read/write splitting routes write operations to the primary and read operations to a replica using a single logical datasource that dynamically chooses the physical connection. In Spring this is typically a custom `AbstractRoutingDataSource` whose routing key is derived per request or from `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, with a `ThreadLocal` holding the current route. The main hazard is replication lag causing stale reads, so any read that must reflect a just-committed write is explicitly routed back to the primary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank has one main ledger (primary) for all changes and several photocopy desks (replicas) for quick enquiries. A smart receptionist (the routing datasource) looks at each request: "Are you changing money? Go to the main ledger. Just checking a balance? Go to a photocopy desk." But if you just made a change, the receptionist knows the photocopies may be a second behind, so for your immediate enquiry she sends you back to the main ledger so you always see your own change.

**One line to remember:** Mark reads as readOnly so a routing datasource sends them to a replica and everything else to the primary, but send must-be-fresh reads back to the primary because of lag.

sections.s2_technical:
The goal is to let a read-heavy banking application offload read traffic to replicas without changing every repository call. You achieve this with one logical datasource that transparently picks the right physical connection.

Spring provides `AbstractRoutingDataSource`, which holds a map of target datasources keyed by a lookup value and overrides `determineCurrentLookupKey()` to decide which one to use for the current operation. You register two targets, PRIMARY and REPLICA, and implement the lookup to read a value from a `ThreadLocal` context holder.

The cleanest way to set that context is to piggyback on `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`. Spring exposes whether the current transaction is read-only via `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly()`. So `determineCurrentLookupKey()` simply returns REPLICA when the transaction is read-only and PRIMARY otherwise. Then you annotate read service methods with `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` and write methods with plain `@Transactional`, and routing happens automatically with no per-call wiring. An alternative is an interceptor or aspect that sets the `ThreadLocal` route based on the HTTP method or an explicit annotation, which you must clear after the request to avoid leaking the route to the next request on a reused thread.

A subtlety: the datasource is chosen when the transaction begins and the connection is acquired, so the routing decision must be made before the connection is bound. With the readOnly approach this works because Spring reads the readOnly flag at transaction start. You also want lazy connection acquisition so the route is resolved at the right moment.

The thing you must watch for is replication lag causing stale reads. Because replicas apply the primary's changes asynchronously, a read routed to a replica immediately after a write may miss that write. For most reads this is fine, but for reads that must be fresh — a balance shown right after a transfer, a confirmation screen, a read-your-own-writes scenario — you must route back to the primary. You do this by not marking those specific reads readOnly, or by a session-consistency mechanism that pins a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write. You also must ensure writes never accidentally run on a replica, since replicas are read-only and will error; the default route must be PRIMARY so anything not explicitly a read goes to the primary. Finally, monitor replication lag and have the routing fall back to the primary if a replica falls too far behind or is unavailable, so stale or failed reads do not surface to customers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, balance checks and statement reads vastly outnumber transfers, and all of them hit the primary, overloading it. This is exactly what read/write splitting fixes — send reads to replicas.

Problem 2 — We do not want to rewire hundreds of repository calls. This is exactly what `AbstractRoutingDataSource` plus `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` solves — routing by annotation, transparently.

Problem 3 — A customer's balance read right after a transfer must not come from a lagging replica. This is exactly the stale-read hazard — that specific read is routed back to the primary.

We will build a `RoutingDataSource` keyed by the readOnly flag, a context holder, read service methods marked readOnly that land on the replica, write methods that land on the primary, and a fresh-read method that deliberately uses the primary.

```
rw-splitting-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/rw/
│   ├── RwApplication.java
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- Same schema on primary and replica; replica is read-only and replays WAL.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance    DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('SAV2001', 1000000.00), ('CUR3001', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    primary:
      jdbc-url: jdbc:postgresql://primary:5432/bankdb
      username: bank_app
      password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    replica:
      jdbc-url: jdbc:postgresql://replica:5432/bankdb
      username: bank_ro
      password: ${DB_RO_PASSWORD}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/rw-splitting-service-1.0.0.jar

# Writes → primary; normal reads → replica; fresh reads → primary
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfer?from=SAV2001&to=CUR3001&amount=50000"  # PRIMARY
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/balance/CUR3001"        # REPLICA (offloaded)
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/balance/CUR3001/fresh"  # PRIMARY (no stale read)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer, a normal balance read, and a must-be-fresh balance read.

Step 1: Transfer. `AccountService.transfer` is annotated plain `@Transactional`, so the transaction is not read-only. When the transaction begins, `RoutingDataSource.determineCurrentLookupKey` sees not-readOnly and returns PRIMARY. The updates run on the primary.

Step 2: Normal balance read. `balance` is annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`. At transaction start, the routing key resolves to REPLICA, so the read is served from a replica, offloading the primary. This is where the scalability win comes from, because reads dominate.

Step 3: The `LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy` ensures the physical connection, and therefore the route, is chosen only when the query actually runs, after the readOnly flag is known.

Step 4: Must-be-fresh read. `freshBalance` deliberately sets the `ThreadLocal` route to PRIMARY before querying, overriding the default. This is used right after a write so the customer sees their own change despite replication lag. The route is cleared in a finally block so the next request on this thread is not accidentally pinned to the primary.

Step 5: The default target is PRIMARY, so if any code path is neither clearly a read nor sets a route, it safely lands on the primary rather than erroring on a read-only replica.

```
2026-10-25 13:52:00 INFO  AccountService - transfer 50000 SAV2001->CUR3001 on PRIMARY
2026-10-25 13:52:00 INFO  AccountService - fresh balance CUR3001 read from PRIMARY = 300000.00
2026-10-25 13:52:05 INFO  AccountService - balance CUR3001 read from REPLICA = 300000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request
    │
    ▼
  @Transactional(readOnly = ?)  → sets TransactionSynchronizationManager flag
    │
    ▼
  RoutingDataSource.determineCurrentLookupKey()
    │
    ├─ forced route set? ──→ use it (freshBalance → PRIMARY)
    │
    ├─ readOnly == true  ──→ REPLICA   (balance checks, statements)  ← offload
    │
    └─ readOnly == false ──→ PRIMARY   (transfers, writes)           ← default
    ▼
  LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy → acquires the chosen physical connection
    │
    ├──────────────┐
    ▼              ▼
  PRIMARY       REPLICA
  (writes +     (most reads)
   fresh reads)
       ▲ WAL replication (async, lag) ──────┘
  WATCH: stale read on replica → route must-be-fresh reads back to PRIMARY
```

```
  ═══ HLD — App-Level Read/Write Splitting ═══

  ┌────────────┐  REST  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Clients    │───────→│ Service (Spring)              │
  └────────────┘        │  RoutingDataSource            │
                        │  key = readOnly ? REPLICA:PRIMARY│
                        └──────┬──────────────┬──────────┘

                           │ (PG)     │══│ (PG, WAL)    │ async lag
                           └──────────┘  └──────────────┘

  Monitor lag → if replica too far behind/unavailable → fall back to PRIMARY
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — RoutingDataSource ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy (route selection) + ThreadLocal context        │
  │ Proxy (LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy defers acquisition)│
  │   WHY: transparent routing by annotation, no rewiring   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RoutingDataSource                     │
  │  extends AbstractRoutingDataSource     │
  │  + determineCurrentLookupKey(): Object │ → PRIMARY | REPLICA
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                  │ reads
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ DbContextHolder (ThreadLocal) │   │ TransactionSynchronization │
  │ + set/get/clear(Route)        │   │ Manager.isReadOnly()       │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────┘

  ── Routing Decision ────────────────────────────────
  forced route?  → use it            (freshBalance)
  else readOnly? → REPLICA           (balance, statements)
  else           → PRIMARY (default) (transfers, writes)

  Watch-list:
    - clear ThreadLocal after request (no route leak)
    - default target = PRIMARY (writes never hit read-only replica)
    - must-be-fresh reads → PRIMARY (replication lag)
    - fall back to PRIMARY if replica lag/unavailable
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I implement read/write splitting at the application level with a single logical datasource that transparently chooses the physical connection, so a read-heavy banking app can offload reads to replicas without rewiring every repository call. In Spring the tool is AbstractRoutingDataSource, which holds a map of targets — PRIMARY and REPLICA — and overrides determineCurrentLookupKey to pick one for the current operation.

The cleanest trigger is the transaction read-only flag. Spring exposes whether the current transaction is read-only through TransactionSynchronizationManager, so my routing key returns REPLICA when the transaction is read-only and PRIMARY otherwise. Then I simply annotate read service methods with Transactional readOnly true and write methods with plain Transactional, and routing happens automatically. I wrap the routing datasource in a LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the physical connection, and therefore the route, is chosen only when the query actually runs, after the read-only flag is known. I also keep a ThreadLocal context holder so I can force a specific route when I need to, and I always set the default target to PRIMARY so that anything not clearly a read lands on the primary rather than erroring on a read-only replica.

The thing I watch for is replication lag causing stale reads. Because replicas apply changes asynchronously, a read sent to a replica right after a write may miss that write. For most reads that is fine, but for reads that must be fresh — a balance shown immediately after a transfer, a confirmation screen, any read-your-own-writes case — I route back to the primary, either by not marking that read read-only or by pinning the user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write. I also must clear the ThreadLocal after each request so a route does not leak onto the next request on a reused thread, and I monitor lag so the routing can fall back to the primary if a replica drifts too far behind or becomes unavailable.

At the National Bank of India, balance checks and statements vastly outnumbered transfers and were overloading the primary. I introduced a routing datasource keyed by the read-only flag, so writes and must-be-fresh reads went to the primary while the flood of ordinary reads went to replicas, with no change to our repository code beyond annotations. The one rule I always emphasize is that reads which must reflect a just-committed write are explicitly routed back to the primary, because replication lag would otherwise show the customer stale data.
